cases.title: Additive particle 도 after a name
cases.why: The additive particle 도 ('also'); one syllable that is also a given-name syllable (도윤, 도현).

cases.title: Comitative 과 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: Partner of the previous case: 과 follows a consonant, and the second name takes 는.

cases.title: Comitative 와 after a vowel-final name, then subject 이
cases.why: Two names joined by a comitative particle whose form depends on the first name's last sound; the second name takes a subject marker.

cases.title: Casual comitative 이랑 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: Partner of the previous case: 이랑 after a consonant-final name. The leading 이 must not be read as part of the name.

cases.title: Casual comitative 랑 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: Colloquial comitative: 랑 after vowels and 이랑 after consonants. Casual speech patterns are common in informal text.

cases.title: Role-change 으로 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: Role-change/instrumental 으로 (consonant) vs 로 (vowel or ㄹ); the particle after a person name marks a new role holder.

cases.title: Role-change 로 after a ㄹ-final name
cases.why: Names ending in the consonant ㄹ take 로, not 으로; the regular consonant rule would predict 으로 and a pattern built on it would miss this.

cases.title: Role-change 로 after a full name ending in ㄹ
cases.why: A three-syllable name whose last syllable ends in ㄹ and takes 로.

cases.title: Role-change 로 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: Partner of allomorph-direction-eu-ro: 로 after a vowel-final name.

cases.title: Object marker 을 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: Partner of allomorph-object-after-vowel: the consonant-final counterpart.

cases.title: Object marker 를 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: Vowel-final names take 를, consonant-final names take 을; here the object marker follows a vowel.

cases.title: Topic marker 은 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: Partner of allomorph-topic-after-vowel: consonant-final names take 은. Minimal pair for the 는/은 allomorph.

cases.title: Topic marker 는 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: Vowel-final names take 는 (not 은). The particle is excluded from the span; a heuristic keyed on 은 alone would miss it.

cases.title: Alternative particle 이나 after a name
cases.why: A two-syllable alternative particle ('or') that starts with the common syllable 이.

cases.title: Alternative 이나 and subject marker after two names
cases.why: 이나 ('or') after a consonant-final name and 이 after a second consonant-final name.

cases.title: Appositive 이자 after a name
cases.why: 이자 joins two roles of one person ('X, who is also the CEO'); it begins with 이.

cases.title: Colloquial comitatives 랑 and 이랑 across two names
cases.why: Both colloquial 'with' allomorphs in one sentence, after a vowel-final and a consonant-final name respectively.

cases.title: Comparative 보다 and subject 이 across two names
cases.why: Two names with different particles in a comparison; the first ends at 보다, the second at 이.

cases.title: Comparative particle 처럼 after a name
cases.why: The two-syllable particle 처럼 ('like') attached to a name used as a role model.

cases.title: Concessive 이든 and 든 after two names
cases.why: 이든 after a consonant-final name and 든 after a vowel-final name; both start with a copula-like syllable.

cases.title: Conjunctive 와 and topic 은 across two full names
cases.why: Two different particles around two names in one sentence: the span of each name ends at its own particle.

cases.title: Attributive 이라는 naming construction
cases.why: 'A person called X' with 이라는; the construction begins with 이 and continues into a noun.

cases.title: Coordinating copula 이며 after a name
cases.why: 이며 coordinates two clauses; the name is the predicate nominal of the first, and the second clause is about a different role holder.

cases.title: Formal copula 입니다 after a self-introduction
cases.why: In an introduction the name is the predicate nominal of 입니다 ('I am X'); the copula starts with the syllable 입.

cases.title: Polite copula 입니다 after a name
cases.why: The polite copula attaches directly to a vowel-final name; it is a verb form and is excluded from the span.

cases.title: Copula 인데 after a name
cases.why: The copula-plus-connective 인데 attached to a name, introducing a clause.

cases.title: Emphatic copula 이야 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: '김민석이야' with 이야 as an emphatic copula; it overlaps the vocative reading, so a boundary choice is needed. Here the sentence is a statement.
cases.text: 이 일을 맡은 사람은 바로 김민석이야.

ambiguity.note: 'The person who took this on is Kim Min-seok' is a copula statement, so 이야 is not a vocative.

cases.title: Plain copula 이다 after a name
cases.why: The plain-style copula 이다 begins with 이 and follows a consonant-final name directly.

cases.title: Quotative 이라고 in a self-introduction
cases.why: 이라고 ('saying that it is') after a name quotes the name itself; it starts with 이, a frequent name syllable.

cases.title: Quotative 라고 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: Partner of copula-quotative-introduction: 라고 (no 이) after a vowel-final name.

cases.title: Directional dative 에게로 after a name
cases.why: A compound particle 에게로 ('towards') after a name; compound particles are longer than usual.

cases.title: Directional 으로 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: The directional/instrumental particle 으로 after a consonant-final name; 으 alone could be read as a name syllable.

cases.title: Directional 로 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: The vowel-final allomorph 로 after a name.

cases.title: Emphatic 이야말로 after a name
cases.why: 이야말로 ('indeed') is a long emphatic particle beginning with 이.

cases.title: Particle 조차 after a name
cases.why: A two-syllable particle ('even') that is also the first syllable of 조 as a surname in other contexts.

cases.title: Particle 마저 after a name
cases.why: A two-syllable particle ('even/also') that starts with the surname syllable 마.

cases.title: Genitive after an honorific suffix
cases.why: Name, spaced 씨, then 의: the name boundary stops before the honorific, not before the genitive.

cases.title: Genitive 의 linking a name to a possessed noun
cases.why: 의 marks the name as possessor; it is excluded from the span like any particle.

cases.title: Organization genitive before a role and a name
cases.why: A company noun plus 의 plus role plus name; the organization is not a person and the name is the last token before the particle.

cases.title: Honorific subject marker 께서 after a name and a title
cases.why: 께서 is the honorific subject marker; it follows the title, not the name directly.

cases.title: Limit particle 까지 after a name
cases.why: The two-syllable particle 까지 ('even/up to') after a name.

cases.title: Object marker 을 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: Object allomorph 을 after a consonant-final name; completes the 을/를 pair.

cases.title: Object marker 를 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: Object allomorph 를 after a vowel-final name in the middle of the sentence.

cases.title: Possessive 의 after a full name
cases.why: The possessive 의 attached to a full name before the noun it modifies.

cases.title: Quotative 이라고 after a name
cases.why: The quotative particle 이라고 after a consonant-final name; the placeholder name 홍길동 is a fictional literary character used generically, not a real person.

cases.title: Rare surname with a name ending in 은 and a topic marker
cases.why: The given name ends in 은, same as the topic marker. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare surname in a formal introduction
cases.why: The copula 입니다 after a rare three-syllable name. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare surname with genitive 의
cases.why: Genitive after a rare name marks a possessor. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare surname with 이라는
cases.why: Attributive naming construction after a rare name. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare surname with 를
cases.why: Object marker after a rare vowel-final name. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare surname with 으로부터
cases.why: Long source marker after a rare consonant-final name. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare surname with stacked 에게는
cases.why: A stack of particles after a rare name. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare surname with stacked 한테도
cases.why: Colloquial stack after a rare name. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Rare surname with 은 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: A rare surname carries no frequency cue, so the boundary must come from the particle alone.

cases.title: Rare surname with 는 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: Partner of rare-surname-topic-consonant: the vowel-final allomorph with a rare surname. The surname is uncommon in Korean, so name frequency gives no cue and the boundary must come from the structure.

cases.title: Restrictive particle 만 after a name
cases.why: The restrictive particle 만 ('only'), a syllable that is also used inside given names.

cases.title: Copula written against the name
cases.why: Article 41 treats 이다/입니다 like a particle that is written against the word before it; the copula is outside the span.

cases.title: Particle written against the name
cases.why: Article 41 writes a particle against the word before it, so the particle is attached but is not part of the name span.

cases.title: Two particles in sequence written against the name
cases.why: Article 41 explains that consecutive particles are written against the preceding word; the whole stack is outside the span.

cases.title: Ablative 에게서 after a name
cases.why: A three-syllable particle sequence (에게서) after a name; longer particle strings are easy to mis-split at the wrong syllable.

cases.title: Colloquial ablative 한테서 after a name
cases.why: A colloquial 'from' particle after a name; it contains the dative 한테 as a prefix, so a greedy particle list can mis-split it.

cases.title: Stacked 에게만 after a name
cases.why: Dative 에게 plus the restrictive particle 만 ('only'); the two-particle stack is excluded as a unit.

cases.title: Stacked 에게는 after a name
cases.why: A dative marker followed by the topic marker 는; the stack is a two-particle stack of three syllables and must be excluded as a unit.

cases.title: Stacked 한테도 after a name
cases.why: Colloquial dative 한테 plus the additive particle 도; the stack is excluded as a unit from the span.

cases.title: Stacked 한테서도 after a name
cases.why: Colloquial source marker 한테서 plus additive 도 after a person name; a person is a source with 한테서, not with 에서.

cases.title: Stacked 으로부터 after a name
cases.why: A long source marker 으로부터 ('from') after a consonant-final name.

cases.title: Stacked 까지도 after a name
cases.why: Terminal 까지 plus additive 도 ('even up to').

cases.title: Starting-point particle 부터 after a name
cases.why: The particle 부터 ('starting from') after a name, in an imperative sentence.

cases.title: Subject marker 가 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: Subject allomorph 가 after a vowel; 가 is itself a very common syllable inside names, so the span must stop at the particle.

cases.title: Subject marker 이 after a consonant-final name
cases.why: Subject allomorph 이 after a consonant; 이 is also a common surname and the demonstrative 'this'.

cases.title: Topic marker 는 after a vowel-final name
cases.why: The vowel-final topic allomorph 는; with 은 covered separately, both allomorph families of the topic marker are represented.

cases.title: Particle sequence 은커녕 after a name
cases.why: A complex particle 은커녕 ('let alone') that begins with the topic marker 은.
